cur:monumental-san-arrest.summary: The bearded Christ, in purple, stands at the centre of a tightly packed group of men who grasp his arms and lead him away, against a background of rocky landscape. It follows the panel of Judas's kiss in the Passion sequence of the south wall and presents Christ calm and unresisting in the hands of his captors.
facts: On the south wall the thirteen Passion and Resurrection scenes show Christ bearded; the cycle omits both the Flagellation and the Crucifixion.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

cur:objects-lateran-acheropita.summary: Behind silver doors in the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum stands Rome's most revered image of Christ, a full-length enthroned Saviour now almost entirely encased in an embossed silver revetment, through which only his painted face looks out. Venerated as 'acheiropoieta', not made by human hands, it was carried in solemn procession through Rome for centuries. What the viewer sees today is the face of Christ framed by the goldsmith's work of Pope Innocent III.
facts: Wikipedia records the tradition that the icon was begun by St Luke and completed by an angel, hence its name 'acheiropoieta' ('not made by human hands').
The silver casing and doors seen in the photograph were added under Pope Innocent III (1198–1216), according to the photographer's caption.
cur:objects-lateran-acheropita.notes: The original panel's date is uncertain (often placed in the 6th–7th century); the face currently visible has been repainted, and most of the image is hidden by the c. 1200 silver revetment.

walters:71.294.summary: Two scenes are stacked on this broken ivory panel. Above, Christ is carried heavenward in a mandorla held by two angels while the Virgin stands at the centre among the apostles, who look up in wonder; below, Christ hangs on the cross between angels, with the soldiers and mourners beneath. The panel joins the Passion to its fulfilment in the Ascension.
facts: The Walters notes that in the Crucifixion the sun and moon, and Stephaton and Longinus, are reversed from their usual positions, and that Longinus carries a sword rather than a spear.
The museum relates its style to the Nikephoros Group of Byzantine ivories.
'AVE MARIA' was scratched on the back, which also bears the impression of a 17th-century seal; the panel belonged to Count Grigorii Stroganov in Rome before 1900.
